approachQuestion.prompt:
A read-only array contains unsigned 32-bit access codes. Choose two different indices and return the largest XOR value of their codes. Repeated codes are allowed. Prioritize worst-case processing time; additional storage is permitted.

Constraints: 2 <= n <= 200000; 0 <= code[i] < 2^32. Return only the maximum value.
Example: [3,10,5] -> 15, from 10 XOR 5. Edge case: [7,7] -> 0.

Choose the best approach under these constraints.
constraints: 32-bit shifts, XOR, comparison and bit tests cost constant time; 32 is fixed, not a size parameter. Trie nodes each have two child indices; allocating a node costs constant time. No input copy is implicit.
Inputs are read-only. Include all temporary storage and any call stack; exclude the supplied input and the returned output. No input copy is implicit.

options.text: Insert the first code in a binary trie of 32 levels. For each later code, greedily query opposite bits from high to low to maximize XOR, update the best, then insert it.
options.feedback: A higher XOR bit outweighs every lower bit. Querying only previously inserted codes ensures different indices even when codes repeat.

options.text: Compute XOR for every pair of different indices and keep the maximum.
options.feedback: This is correct and uses less storage, but enumerates all index pairs. With the fixed 32-bit width, sharing trie prefixes improves the worst-case processing time, which is the stated priority.

options.text: Return the XOR of the numerically smallest and largest codes.
options.feedback: For [2,5,6], the numeric extremes give 2 XOR 6 = 4, while 2 XOR 5 = 7 is larger.

options.text: Build a binary trie, preferring the same bit at each level when querying a code.
options.feedback: Preferring agreement minimizes XOR rather than maximizing it; querying a trie containing 3 and 10 for 5 can choose 3, giving 6 instead of 15.

feedback.reason: Greedily taking an opposite trie bit maximizes the highest remaining XOR position, outweighing every lower bit.
details: Keep a binary trie of earlier codes. At each of its 32 levels, prefer an existing child opposite to the query bit, because that gives the highest remaining XOR bit. Insert the current code only after querying.

Greedily taking an opposite trie bit maximizes the highest remaining XOR position, outweighing every lower bit. Query before insertion to enforce different indices. The trie stores earlier codes, not just the current best result.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For query-before-trie-insert, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n be the number of codes; the word width is fixed at 32.
constraints: 32-bit shifts, XOR, comparison and bit tests cost constant time; 32 is fixed, not a size parameter. Trie nodes each have two child indices; allocating a node costs constant time. No input copy is implicit.
Inputs are read-only. Include all temporary storage and any call stack; exclude the supplied input and the returned output. No input copy is implicit.

feedback.reason: Two 32-level trie walks per code create at most linear many nodes.
details: Each code traverses 32 levels for insertion and query, so time is linear in n. At most 32n trie nodes are created, and legal inputs with many distinct codes require a linear number of leaves. Nodes, indices and no recursive stack give linear auxiliary storage.

32-bit shifts, XOR, comparison and bit tests cost constant time; 32 is fixed, not a size parameter. Trie nodes each have two child indices; allocating a node costs constant time. No input copy is implicit.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This is the pairwise alternative, which does not share prefix work.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This omits the trie nodes retained for prior codes.
“O(1) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Every input must be considered in the worst case, even though each word has fixed width.
